title: LED bulb: take out the LED board, driver and heat sink
summary: A mains LED bulb holds an aluminium LED board and a small driver board in its base, and many dead bulbs have only one failed part, so test before you strip one. Allow about 10 minutes. The driver connects straight to the mains and its capacitor can keep a charge: open the bulb out of its socket and discharge the driver before you touch the board.

steps.text: Switch the power off at the breaker and unscrew the bulb from its socket. Set aside any bulb that still lights: it is worth more as a bulb than as parts. Bulbs that flicker or have one dark segment can often be fixed (see notes).

Look at the bulb and its label. Most have a frosted dome over a metal or plastic-coated body (the heat sink) with a screw cap at the bottom. The label gives volts and watts. 'Smart' bulbs have a radio board as well. Clear glass bulbs with thin yellow rods inside are filament types: see notes.

Remove the dome. Rest the bulb on a table, slide a thin blade into the seam between dome and body and work it round, twisting a little at a time. Most domes are snapped on or glued with a ring of silicone: cut through the glue as you go.
steps.warn: Domes crack into sharp pieces. Cut away from your hand, wear glasses and don't hold the bulb in your palm.

steps.text: Lift out the LED board: a disc or ring of aluminium with a ring of white chips, held by screws, clips or heat-sink glue. Two thin wires lead from it to the driver in the base. Cut each wire about 3 cm from the board, or desolder them. If the board comes away stuck to the heat sink, leave it there.

Take off the base. The screw cap is crimped or glued to the neck: twist it with pliers while pulling to break the glue, or cut the two thin wires that join the driver to the cap and the bottom contact. Slide the driver board out of the neck, holding it by the board edges.
steps.warn: The driver's capacitor may still hold a charge. Keep fingers off its leads and solder points until you have discharged it in the next step.

steps.text: Discharge the driver: touch your discharge tool across the leads of its biggest capacitor (a small black can, or a block in a plastic case) for 10 seconds, then measure across it with the meter set to DC volts. You want less than 1 V (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: If the bleed resistor has failed, the capacitor can hold mains-level voltage for days. Don't touch the board until the meter reads under 1 V.

steps.text: Test the LED board. Touch a 9 V battery through a 470 ohm resistor across one chip's two pads at a time (the pads are marked + and -). A good chip lights. A chip that stays dark is dead. Chips with several dice in one package need 6-12 V and may glow dimly or not at all on 9 V: try 12 V through a 1 kilohm resistor.

Test the driver without mains: set the meter to continuity or ohms and check the small blue or brown fusible resistor near the input wires. It should read a few ohms. Open means it has blown, and a bulb with a blown fusible resistor is often fixable by replacing it with a similar resistor.
Keep the LED board on a heat sink: chips fail fast without one. If you remove the board, bolt it to a piece of aluminium or steel with a thin smear of grease or paste between them.

Keep each bulb's board and driver together and note on a label how many chips the board has and whether the driver and board both tested good. A driver is built to run its own board: mixing pairs is a good way to burn out LEDs.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **LED board.** A cheap, bright light source: a good bulb board gives several hundred lumens from a few watts. It is the part most worth keeping.
- **Driver.** A small mains power supply that turns 120-240 V into a steady low current for the LEDs. Reuse it only with its own board, in its own case, and treat it as a mains device: don't run it open or in wet places.
- **Heat sink.** The aluminium body carries heat away from the board. Keep it with the board.

## Fixing a dead bulb

- One dead chip in a series string stops all the chips in the string. Join its two pads with a blob of solder or a short wire and the rest light again. The chips either side then run slightly warmer, so keep the bulb on its heat sink.
- A blown fusible resistor near the input is the next most common fault.
- A bad driver capacitor makes a bulb flicker or fail to light at all. Swap in a capacitor with the same value and voltage if you have one.

## Running a board on 12 V

A bare LED board will burn out if you connect it straight to a battery. Use a resistor or constant-current driver sized for the board, as shown in build_led_lighting_12v. Find a board's voltage by lighting it through a resistor on a current-limited supply and measuring across it.

## Variations

- Filament-style LED bulbs have thin glass rods in a sealed glass bulb and a small driver in the base. The rods are fragile; keep the bulb whole or use it as it is.
- Spot and downlight bulbs have a bigger heat sink and often a separate low-voltage driver in the fitting.
- Smart bulbs add a radio board. It is tiny and not reusable without its maker's app, so leave it.

## What to leave

- The plastic dome and base.
- Any driver you can't discharge to under 1 V.
